title: The spring ships
learnerQuestion: Who sailed into Manila each spring around 1602, what did they bring and what did they take home, and how much silver went with them?
sensitiveContentNotice: One part of this Story, "The massacre of 1603", describes the killing of many Chinese residents of Manila, and people forced to row in a war fleet.

paragraphs.text: Every spring the ships came in from China.
Morga, writing in 1609, said that thirty usually came each year, and sometimes forty, most often at the new moon of March.
They made the crossing in fifteen or twenty days, and sailed home before the gales at the end of May.
The count historians use for 1602 has eighteen Chinese ships, not thirty.
No Source we have read explains the difference.
What those ships carried, what they took home, and how much of it there was, is the Story.
Morga wrote that the ships carried the great merchants who owned the goods, their servants, and agents for other merchants who stayed in China.
They came with leave from their own officials. In 1589 the Ming court had fixed the number of ship licences, and sixteen were for Luzon.
Once a cargo had been listed and valued, it was taken to the Chinese quarter (the Parián) or to other warehouses outside the city, and sold there freely.
Historians agree that the Chinese of Manila had grown from about forty people in 1570 to many thousands by 1600.
They do not agree on how many.
Morga listed what the ships brought. Raw silk came first, then velvets and brocades.
The list runs on to fine crockery, furniture, and caged birds, some that talked and some that sang.
What went back was silver. Morga says the Chinese traders were paid in silver and reals, because they wanted neither gold nor other goods.
A Chinese official said the same. In 1604 the governor of Fujian, Xu Xueju, wrote that his people traded at Luzon only for the silver coins to be had there.
We have his words in a historian's translation.
On each cargo the king's officers took three per cent.
In 1593 the crown set a limit. Morga wrote that no more than five hundred thousand in coin was to be sent from New Spain to the Philippines each year.
It was not kept. About 1602 a Manila lawyer, Fernández de Castro, wrote that the royal decrees limiting the trade were not observed.

The crown also tried to keep Peru out of the trade altogether. In 1582 it forbade direct trade between Peru and the Philippines. From 1604 it cut the trade between Peru and New Spain down ship by ship, and in 1631 it forbade it.
Citizens of Mexico and Peru, Fernández de Castro wrote, brought over so much money that Manila's own citizens were crowded out of the ships.
Most of the money on record was private. Of the silver registered at Acapulco for the Philippines in 1601 to 1610, about three-quarters was private money and a quarter the king's.
How much silver was it? The figures do not agree.
In 1586 an official at Manila, Pedro de Rojas, told the king that three hundred thousand pesos went to China every year, and more than five hundred thousand that year.
In 1602 the city council of Mexico City told the king that three million a year went to the Philippines, and more than twelve million in five years.

Historians long quoted the letter as five million a year and twelve million in 1597, which the minute does not say. No other source confirms the council's figures, and the council was asking for the trade to be closed.
Manila's customs duties point to about one million pesos a year leaving on Chinese ships in 1601 to 1605.
The historian who worked that out thinks the true figure could be three or four times as much, because so much went unrecorded.
Historians of the silver trade explain all this by China's demand for silver: it was worth more in Ming China than anywhere else.
That is the mainstream explanation, and it is an interpretation. The Claim beneath each sentence says whose voice it rests on.
One thread runs back to Potosí. A historian of the town writes that a description made in 1603 counted twenty-four shops for European dry goods, and that such shops also sold Chinese silk.
It shows Chinese goods at Potosí. It does not show Potosí silver at Manila.
In October 1603 there was fighting at Manila between Chinese residents and the Spaniards.
It ended in the killing of very many of the Chinese of Manila, by Spanish soldiers and by the Japanese and Philippine troops who fought beside them.
Spanish and Chinese records tell the same events in the same order.
They do not read them the same way.
Both name one visit as what set off the Spaniards' fear of an invasion: in May 1603 three Ming officials came to Manila to look for a mountain said to yield gold.
The Chinese records begin their account ten years earlier.
In 1593 two hundred and fifty Chinese were forced to row in a Spanish war fleet; they mutinied and killed the governor.

beats.sensitiveNotice: This part describes the killing of Chinese residents of Manila in 1603, and people forced to row in a war fleet in 1593.

cells.text: The Spanish writers say the Chinese of Manila rose.
Archbishop Benavides wrote that a rumour had spread among them that the Spaniards meant to kill them all.
The Chinese records say the Spaniards prepared the killing.
They say the Chinese fled when they learned of a plan to kill them.

segments.text: José Eugenio Borao, who set the Spanish and Chinese records side by side, writes that the reasons for the uprising remain unclear.

cells.text: Governor Acuña wrote that he had a ditch dug where the Chinese quarter (the Parián) stood, along the whole front from the river to the sea.
They say the Spaniards bought up the iron the Chinese owned, and made them register their names in groups of three hundred.
Governor Acuña told the king it had been stirred up from China.
The Chinese records put the first blame on one of their own, Zhang Yi.
The Ming emperor, in the official history, said that the governor of Luzon had killed people without leave.

segments.text: A historian notes that the testimony behind the governor's charge was taken under torture.

rows.label: How many were killed

cells.text: The official history of the Ming gives twenty-five thousand in one place and twenty thousand in another.
A second Chinese work speaks of ten thousand killed in a single ambush.

emptyCellText: No count of the dead from the Spanish records is in the Sources we have read.

segments.text: The historian José Eugenio Borao writes 'some 20,000'.

cells.text: The Spanish account has thirteen ships from China at Manila in May 1604.
The governor of Fujian, Xu Xueju, wrote to Manila demanding that the widows and children of the dead be sent home.

provenanceLine.text: The Chinese records reach us through one historian, José Eugenio Borao, who translated them. So do the Spanish records here, except one letter of the governor's, which we read in Blair and Robertson's translation.

closingParagraphs.text: The customs count has fifteen ships from China at Manila for 1604.
Xu Xueju is the same official who wrote, in 1604, that his people went to Luzon only for the silver.

paragraphs.text: **Not yet researched.** This Story stops in 1604, when the ships came back. What the trade became after that, what the silver did in China beyond the ships' home port, and what Chinese goods did in Peru have not been researched, so none is offered as a researched path. When a path is researched, it will appear here with its own Claims and Evidence.

momentLinks.honestyLine: The same port, twenty-nine years apart. No researched Connection joins the two Stories. They share some Sources, Morga among them.

momentLinks.label: Another moment: Potosí, 1573
momentLinks.honestyLine: A researched Connection joins Peru's silver and Manila for about 1590 to 1604, some twenty years after the Potosí Story. Silver from Peru went by sea to Acapulco for Chinese goods, and most of it was sent on to Manila. The letters of the time say Peru. That Potosí silver was in it is one historian's reading, Kris Lane's, and he writes that how much is uncertain.

momentLinks.label: Another moment: Macao, 1590
momentLinks.honestyLine: Two routes by which silver reached China, twelve years apart. No researched Connection joins the two Stories. They share some Sources, von Glahn among them.

momentLinks.label: Another moment: Haicheng, 1602
momentLinks.honestyLine: The home port of the ships, in the same year. That Story's Connection begins here, at Manila: it tells what the port did when the ships came back with coin. They share Sources, von Glahn and Borao among them.
